---
title: "Where are the modern Renaissance men and women?"
date: '2026-10-06'
---

Imagine what Leonardo da Vinci would have accomplished if he had lived today with all the productivity tools available to us. If he achieved so much with the limited resources of the 15th century, what more could he have done with tools such as the internet and artificial intelligence?

When ChatGPT was released, venture capitalist Marc Andreessen posed a provocative question on the Lex Fridman podcast: "Where are all the hyper-productive people?" We now have access to AI, a remarkably powerful tool that can patiently answer our questions and help deepen our understanding of virtually any subject. All we need is the curiosity of a Renaissance person. Better yet, these answers are available on demand. We can access them instantly, allowing us to explore a wide variety of topics without investing excessive time in any single one.

Yet the question remains: Why don't we have more Renaissance men and women today?

Elon Musk is often cited as an example of a modern-day Renaissance person. Love him or hate him, he has a full plate, juggling multiple ventures while being handsomely rewarded for his efforts. One only has to look at his net worth. But surely we cannot be satisfied with Musk and a small handful of people being exceptionally productive. We need more Renaissance-minded individuals taking advantage of modern technology to satisfy their curiosity and broaden their skills.

It seems to me that curiosity is at a low point today. We have become a society of consumers rather than producers. We need more people creating things. Yes, we live in a flood of content, but much of that content comes from a relatively small number of individuals. Most people are happier to watch than to participate in the act of creation. They would rather read a book than write one, or listen to a podcast than produce one. This is a surprising phenomenon given the abundance of tools now available to help us create almost anything we can imagine.

Part of the reluctance to indulge our curiosity stems from our desire for a financial payoff. Many of us pursue activities primarily for economic gain. We want to create something not for its beauty, intrinsic value, or enjoyment, but for its ability to generate income. As a result, many people are unwilling to invest significant time in pursuits that offer no clear financial return.

There is no shame in this. We all need to put food on the table. Countless interesting projects have been started and later abandoned because they failed to generate revenue. However, if money is the only fuel that motivates us, we will continue to see a decline in the number of hyper-productive people. I love money too, but even I have to admit that not all of my interests will provide monetary value. Sometimes you have to pursue an idea simply because it fascinates you, fully aware that there may never be any financial reward. In my view, that is one of the essential ingredients of becoming a Renaissance person.
